lesson_title: A Lift to the Centre of the Earth
hook_text: The deepest mine on Earth is in South Africa, and it hasn't even scratched the surface. Here's what lies below.
clip_script: South African miners dig for gold nearly four kilometres underground. Impressive, but the centre of the Earth is about 6 371 kilometres down. Take the lift. First the crust, a thin rocky skin, 5 to 70 kilometres thick. Then the mantle: almost 3 000 kilometres of hot rock so soft it creeps like toffee over millions of years. Next the outer core, an ocean of liquid iron and nickel, swirling to make the magnetic field your compass follows. Finally the inner core, solid metal as hot as the surface of the Sun, kept solid by unimaginable pressure. Nobody has ever been there. We mapped it all by listening to earthquake waves bouncing through the planet.
visual_style: A glass lift dropping through glowing layers with a depth counter; a cut-away Earth like a sliced egg; seismograph lines pulsing across the globe.
pacing: Mine-shaft open, a steady descent layer by layer, a hushed reveal at the core, a clever twist on how we know.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and discover the treasure hidden in South Africa's rocks.
